definition: Expurgate means to remove the offensive or objectionable parts of a text.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word expurgate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know expurgate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The anthology's editors expurgated the sailors' shanties, so the printed verses end two lines before the sailors did.
Soften is far milder than expurgate — the rough joke stays in the text, just eased by a word or two, while expurgating strips the offending passages out entirely.
Cut is stronger than soften but narrower than expurgate: you cut one scene, while expurgating means combing the whole work and stripping every part that could offend.

To censor is for an authority — a state, a school board, a platform — to suppress or forbid content outright, sometimes blocking the whole work. Expurgate is the editor's milder act: the offensive passages are cut, but a cleaned edition still reaches readers.

Bowdlerize means to expurgate prudishly and excessively, scrubbing anything remotely improper — the word mocks Thomas Bowdler's scrubbed Shakespeare. To expurgate is the neutral, professional version; bowdlerizing is the same cutting carried to a fussy, disapproving extreme.

Expurgate means to remove the offensive or objectionable parts of a text.
Before the school broadcast, the drama teacher expurgated the radio play, cutting the duel and the tavern brawl but keeping every turn of the plot intact.
Expurgate is narrower than edit or shorten because it targets only what might offend — the duel and the brawl went, not because the play was too long, but to make a clean version for young ears.
Expurgate is an editor's word, and a precise one: the cuts aim at offense, not length.
Truncate, taught in this unit, shortens by lopping off an end; expunge, also in this unit, annihilates an entry from a record.
Censor is the heavier cousin — an authority forbidding content — where expurgating produces a cleaned edition that still gets published.

When the poet Ines Varga died in 1902, her sister Alba prepared the letters for publication — and prepared them thoroughly.
Alba expurgated the collection before the printer ever saw it, cutting every feud with a rival, every barbed remark about a critic, and every line about money.
The volume that appeared in 1904 was admired for its serenity; readers met a poet who seemed never to have quarreled with anyone.
A century later, scholars located the originals in a bank vault and printed them uncut.
Set side by side, the two editions tell different stories: one a monument, the other a life.
